result:
I've written `note_taker.py` in the project directory. It uses only the standard library. I ran it against a temporary notes directory and the main flows worked. I didn't test the `$EDITOR` path.

**Commands**
- `new TITLE [-t tag,tag] [-b BODY]` creates a note. With no `-b`, it reads the body from piped stdin. In a terminal with neither, it opens `$VISUAL` or `$EDITOR`.
- `list [-t TAG]... [-s KEYWORD]` lists notes, most recently updated first. `-t` is repeatable and requires all the given tags. `-s` matches the title, body or tags, ignoring case.
- `show NOTE [--raw]` prints a note, or the stored file with `--raw`.
- `edit NOTE` opens the note in your editor and refreshes `updated` if you changed it. `--title`, `-t` and `-b` edit it directly instead (`-t` replaces the tags).
- `delete NOTE [-y]` asks for confirmation unless you pass `-y`. When input isn't a terminal, it refuses to delete without `-y`.

**Storage**
- Each note is `~/.note-taker/<slug>.md`, with frontmatter holding `title`, `tags`, `created` and `updated`. Setting `NOTE_TAKER_DIR` changes the directory.
- A `NOTE` argument can be the exact id, an id prefix, or a fragment of the title. If more than one note matches, it lists them and exits.
- The frontmatter is read and written by a small hand-written parser, since there's no YAML library in the standard library. It handles quotes in titles and both `[a, b]` and dash-list tags, but not general YAML.

An edit with `--title` doesn't rename the file, so the id stays the same.
